newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Croat mob throws eggs, blocks Moslem return.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Croat mob throws eggs, blocks Moslem return.

text.p: An angry mob of Bosnian Croats forced a group of Moslem refugees to cancel a ground-breaking return to their home town on Friday, throwing stones and eggs at their bus.
The crowd of some 200 people blocked the main road to the southern town of Stolac when a bus with nine Moslem families arrived for a long-delayed return to their pre-war homes.

Chanting "no more mosques, no more bowing prayers, no more Moslems", the Croats threw eggs indiscriminately at Moslem representatives, U.N. aid workers, officers for the NATO-led peace force and even their own Croat police.
The crowd was comprised of mostly school children and Croat refugees expelled from central towns during the 1992-1995 Bosnian war.

The nine Moslem families, forced out of Stolac by Croat separatists in 1993, were scheduled to return under supervision of U.N. police monitors and peacekeeping troops in the multinational Stabilisation Force (SFOR).
The incident dealt another blow to stalled efforts to bring refugees back to their pre-war homes and underlined persistent tensions within the troubled Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation.

Croats and Moslems began the Bosnian war as allies but waged a vicious war for territory in 1993. They bowed to U.S. pressure the next year and formed a bi-national federation covering half of Bosnia.
The peace treaty that ended the Bosnian war in November 1995 guarantees the right of those displaced by fighting to return home.
More than one year since the peace accords were signed, refugee returns have been held up by lingering mistrust and nationalist policies by all the former warring factions.
"I expected something like this as this return has been postponed many times. This is a very bad sign for the future," said Rasim Kadic, minister for refugees in the Croat-Moslem federation.
"Obviously, even such a small-scale return as this cannot work," he said.
After Kadic failed in his attempts to reach the Croat mayor of Stolac, he ordered the bus to turn around.
As the convoy started pulling away the crowd broke through a police cordon and started running after the vehicles, throwing eggs and rocks.
The Moslems who sat in their bus during the standoff showed no despair at the failure. "I am feeling elated and proud," said 58-year old Vanja Fidika, a dentist.
"I've come back to my hometown and I've seen my apartment. Things will take time to be solved politically, but we'll be back."
